figures.caption: Figure 5.1.6 compares our receivers (narrow band) with blocker-tolerant receivers. Comparing our SE receiver with narrow band receivers [1-2] we use a fraction of the area and power to get better linearity and harmonic rejection and comparable noise. Compared with the best wideband receiver [6] we have a worse noise but better linearity, harmonic rejection and area. In addition we consume 20% less power even though [6] uses an SE LNA also making it more sensitive to coupling. Acknowledgements: This work was supported by the European M. references.sentence: The two receiver chains reported in Fig. 5.1.1 address these issues.
The two LNAs are reported in Fig. 5.1.2.
In the SE LNA (Fig. 5.1.2.a) this is done by a fourth coil with a k of 1, while in the differential LNA (Fig. 5.1.2.b) by a capacitive feed-forward from the input.
A passive current mixer is ac-coupled to the LNA (Fig. 5.1.3).
The four clock phases used to drive the I and Q mixers are generated directly by a divider able to create 25% duty-cycle signals from a differential externally supplied clock at 2fLO (Fig. 5.1.4.a).
The generation of 25% duty-cycle outputs relies on the particular 2011. latch (Fig. 5.1.4.b).
The BB is made-up by a re-configurable TIA (Fig. 5.1.1), implementing a second order filter, whose topology was derived from [4].
Figure 5.1.5.c shows both NF and gain with a blocker 20MHz from the carrier vs. blocker power for TDD.
Figure 5.1.5.d shows 3rd-and 5th-harmonic rejection vs. fLO; 54dB and 65dB are obtained at 2.2 GHz (maximum gain) for TDD.
The die micrograph is shown in Fig. 5.1.7.
